name: Selling Across Borders: Small Traders and the AfCFTA
objectives: Given your product and the country you want to sell to, explain what the AfCFTA and your regional trade scheme can do for a small trader and name the offices to check the current rules with, naming at least two offices or official websites

Before you take goods through an official border crossing, list the papers and steps you need for your goods, such as receipts, an invoice, a customs declaration and a certificate of origin, with every paper on the list checked with customs or a trade desk
Given the costs of one batch and an exchange rate, calculate the full cost per item and a selling price in both currencies, including every cost and a profit, with the arithmetic correct

chapters.name: Chapter 1: The rules and the papers

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the AfCFTA means for a small trader
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words what the AfCFTA is and how it can help your business.
This lesson builds toward: Given your product and the country you want to sell to, you will explain what the AfCFTA and your regional trade scheme can do for a small trader and name the offices to check the current rules with, naming at least two offices or official websites.
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is an agreement among the 55 countries of the African Union to make one big market of about 1.3 billion people. Trading under it started on 1 January 2021. Its Secretariat is in Accra, Ghana.
The main idea: over time, countries that have joined lower or remove import duties on goods made in other member countries, and work to remove other barriers, such as long delays and extra papers. To get the lower duty, your goods must "come from" a member country under the rules of origin. Goods only bought from outside Africa and resold do not qualify.
Not every country applies it in the same way or at the same speed, and not every product is covered yet. The Guided Trade Initiative, launched on 7 October 2022, started real trade under AfCFTA rules in a group of countries. So before you count on a lower duty, check with your customs authority, your trade ministry or chamber of commerce, and the AfCFTA website.
Even where the AfCFTA is not yet working for your product, regional schemes may already help you. That is the next lesson.
Words to know:
- AfCFTA: the African Continental Free Trade Area: an agreement to make Africa one big market with lower duties and fewer barriers.
- Import duty (tariff): a tax a country charges on goods that come in from another country.
- Rules of origin: the rules that decide which country a product "comes from", so it can get the lower duty.
Official sources:
- AfCFTA Secretariat: About the AfCFTA (55 AU countries, trading from 1 January 2021, Secretariat in Accra)
- AfCFTA Secretariat: Guided Trade Initiative (launched 7 October 2022)
- AfCFTA Secretariat: Rules of Origin (Annex 2 and the Rules of Origin Manual)
Try it now: Write down one product you sell or could sell, and one neighbouring country you could sell it to. Then write two places where you will check whether the AfCFTA lowers the duty on that product.
You can now say what the AfCFTA is, how it can help a small trader, and where to check whether it applies to your goods.

check.q: What is the main thing the AfCFTA aims to do for traders?
options: Fix the prices of all goods in Africa
Lower duties and barriers on goods made in member countries
Make one currency for all of Africa
check.why: The AfCFTA aims to lower duties and barriers on goods that come from member countries; it does not fix prices, create one currency or stop checks.

check.q: A trader buys phone covers made outside Africa and wants to resell them next door under the AfCFTA. What is true?
options: They likely do not qualify, because the goods were not made in a member country
They need no papers at all
check.why: Under the rules of origin, goods only bought from outside Africa and resold do not come from a member country.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Regional schemes that already help small traders
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the regional trade scheme for your route and the desk or office that explains it.
This lesson builds toward: Given your product and the country you want to sell to, you will explain what the AfCFTA and your regional trade scheme can do for a small trader and name the offices to check the current rules with, naming at least two offices or official websites.
Before the AfCFTA, Africa's regional economic communities already made trade easier. In West Africa, the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS) lets approved goods from ECOWAS countries move between member states with lower or no duty. Senegal, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria are all ECOWAS members.
In East and Southern Africa, the East African Community (EAC) and COMESA have Simplified Trade Regimes for small traders. They allow small consignments of listed goods to cross with simpler papers, such as a simplified certificate of origin. Some border posts have trade information desks where officers explain the rules to small traders, free of charge.
The value limits, the list of goods and the forms are set by each scheme and can change. Ask the customs office at your crossing, the trade information desk, or your cross-border traders' association. Write down what they tell you, with the date and the officer's name.
Central Africa (for example Cameroon) and North Africa (for example Morocco, Egypt and Tunisia) have their own regional agreements too. Ask your customs authority which ones apply to your route.
Step by step:
- Write your route: from which country, through which crossing, to which country.
- Find the regional community both countries belong to (for example ECOWAS, EAC or COMESA).
- Ask the customs office, trade desk or traders' association which scheme your goods can use.
- Ask: which goods qualify, what value limit applies, and which form or certificate you need.
- Write the answers down with the date and the officer's name.
Words to know:
- Regional economic community: a group of neighbouring countries that work together on trade, for example ECOWAS, EAC or COMESA.
- Simplified Trade Regime: an EAC or COMESA arrangement that lets small traders take small loads of listed goods across with simpler papers.
- Consignment: one load or batch of goods you send or carry.
Official sources:
- ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS), ECOWAS Commission
- COMESA: Trade and Customs (including the Simplified Trade Regime for small traders)
Try it now: For your route from Lesson 1, write the regional community both countries belong to, and three questions you will ask at the customs office or trade desk.
You can now find the regional scheme for your route and ask the right office the right questions about it.

check.q: Which scheme is most likely to apply to a trader taking shea butter from Ghana to Burkina Faso?
check.why: Ghana and Burkina Faso are both in West Africa's ECOWAS region, so ETLS is the scheme to ask about.

check.q: You want to know the value limit for a simplified certificate on your route. What do you do?
options: Ask the customs office or trade desk at the crossing and write the answer down
Guess, because it is the same everywhere
Use the figure from a friend's crossing last year
check.why: Limits differ by scheme and change, so the customs office or trade desk is the place to ask.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The papers you carry at an official crossing
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the papers and steps for taking your goods through an official border crossing.
This lesson builds toward: Before you take goods through an official border crossing, you will list the papers and steps you need for your goods, such as receipts, an invoice, a customs declaration and a certificate of origin, with every paper on the list checked with customs or a trade desk.
Using an official crossing protects you. Your goods are recorded, you can claim lower duties under the schemes, and you have proof if something goes wrong. Goods smuggled through unofficial paths can be seized, and you have no protection.
Common papers include: your ID or passport; a receipt or invoice showing what you bought or made and its value; a list of your goods (a packing list); a customs declaration, which the officer or a clearing agent helps you fill; and a certificate of origin when you want a lower duty. Food, plants, animals, medicines and cosmetics may also need a health, plant (phytosanitary) or product approval certificate.
Some goods are restricted or banned. Ask before you buy stock. A clearing agent can help with bigger loads, but always get a receipt for every official payment, and keep copies of all papers on your phone and on paper.
Example: Awa sells handmade soap from Dakar to Bamako. She asks the customs office which papers she needs, gets her invoice and a certificate of origin, and keeps a photo of each paper. At the border she pays only what is on the official receipt.
Step by step:
- Ask customs which papers your goods need, and whether any are restricted.
- Get receipts or invoices for your goods, and make a packing list.
- Get a certificate of origin if you want a lower duty under a scheme.
- Ask about health, plant or product certificates for food, plants, animals and cosmetics.
- Use the official crossing, fill the customs declaration, and keep a receipt for every payment.
- Keep copies of every paper on paper and as photos on your phone.
Words to know:
- Customs declaration: a form telling customs what goods you carry and their value.
- Certificate of origin: a paper that shows which country your goods come from, so you can get a lower duty.
- Clearing agent: a licensed person or company that helps traders complete customs papers, for a fee.
- Phytosanitary certificate: a plant health certificate for plants, seeds, grains, fruits and vegetables.
Official sources:
- AfCFTA Secretariat: Rules of Origin (Annex 2 and the Rules of Origin Manual)
- ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS), ECOWAS Commission
Try it now: Make a paper checklist for your product and route: every paper you think you need, with a box to tick after customs or the trade desk confirms it.
You can now list the papers and steps you need to take your goods through an official crossing, and keep proof of every payment.

check.q: Which paper helps you claim a lower duty under a trade scheme?
check.why: A certificate of origin shows the goods come from a member country, which is what the lower duty depends on.

check.q: You pay a fee at customs. What should you get?
options: An official receipt, which you keep
A promise to see you next time
check.why: An official receipt is proof of a real fee and protects you if anything goes wrong.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Money, payment and problems at the border

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Costing a cross-border batch in two currencies
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the full cost per item and a selling price in both currencies.
This lesson builds toward: Given the costs of one batch and an exchange rate, you will calculate the full cost per item and a selling price in both currencies, including every cost and a profit, with the arithmetic correct.
Many traders lose money across borders because they count only the cost of the goods. Count everything: the goods, packing, transport to the border and beyond, loading, official duties and fees (checked with customs), clearing agent, storage, your phone and data, your food and lodging on the trip, and a little extra for losses.
Add all costs and divide by the number of items you can really sell. That is your cost per item. Add your profit to get a selling price. Then change it into the buyer's currency using today's exchange rate, and check the price of similar goods in that market.
Example (figures are examples only): Ama buys and packs 100 tubs of shea butter in Tamale for GHS 2,000 in all. Transport, loading and lodging cost GHS 600. Official fees checked at customs: GHS 200. Total GHS 2,800, so GHS 28 per tub. She adds GHS 7 profit: GHS 35. If the day's rate were 1 GHS = 40 XOF, that is 1,400 XOF per tub. She checks that shops in Ouagadougou sell similar tubs for about that price.
Exchange rates move every day. Check the rate on the day you sell and the day you change money, and agree with your buyer which currency the price is in.
Step by step:
- List every cost of the batch, from buying to selling.
- Add them to get the total cost.
- Divide by the number of items you can really sell: cost per item.
- Add your profit: selling price in your currency.
- Change it to the buyer's currency at today's rate, and compare with the market price there.
Words to know:
- Exchange rate: how much of one currency you get for one unit of another, for example how many XOF for 1 GHS.
- Cost per item: the total cost of a batch divided by the number of items you can sell.
- Landed cost: the full cost of goods once they reach the buyer's market, including transport and duties.
Try it now: Cost one batch of your product for your route: list every cost, find the cost per item, add your profit, and write the price in both currencies using today's rate.
You can now work out the full cost per item of a cross-border batch and a selling price in both currencies.

check.q: A batch of 50 bags costs NGN 250,000 in total, including transport and fees. What is the cost per bag?
check.why: 250,000 divided by 50 bags is 5,000 per bag.

check.q: Which cost do traders most often forget?
options: Their own lodging, food and losses on the trip
check.why: Trip costs such as lodging, food and losses are easy to forget, and they eat the profit.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting paid safely across borders
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a safe way to receive payment from a buyer in another country and spot a payment scam.
This lesson builds toward: When a buyer in another country pays you, you will choose a safe way to receive the money and spot the warning signs of a payment scam, never sharing a PIN or sending goods before the money is confirmed.
Cash at the border is risky: you can be robbed, and changing money in the street can give you a bad rate or fake notes. Safer ways include a bank transfer, a mobile money service that sends across borders on your route, and payment systems such as PAPSS (the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System), which lets a payer in one African country pay in local currency and the receiver get local currency, through banks and payment providers that have joined it. Ask your bank or mobile money provider what works on your route and what it costs.
For a new buyer, ask for a deposit before you send, or full payment before you hand over the goods. Check that the money has really arrived in your account, by checking your balance yourself, not by trusting a message the buyer sends you.
Warning signs of a scam: a buyer who sends a fake "payment received" message or screenshot; someone who says they sent too much by mistake and asks you to send the difference back; anyone who asks for your PIN, password or a code sent to your phone; and a buyer who rushes you to release goods before you check. A real bank or mobile money provider never asks for your PIN.
Step by step:
- Agree the price, the currency and the payment method in writing.
- Ask a new buyer for a deposit or full payment first.
- Check your balance yourself to confirm the money arrived.
- Only then release the goods, and give a receipt.
- Never share your PIN, password or a code sent to your phone.
Words to know:
- PAPSS: the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System: lets payments between African countries be made in local currencies, through banks and payment providers that have joined.
- Deposit: part of the price paid before you send the goods.
- PIN: the secret number for your bank card or mobile money account. Never share it.
Official sources:
- Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS)
Try it now: Write the payment rule for your business in three lines: which method you accept, when you release goods, and how you check the money arrived. Ask your bank or mobile money provider which cross-border service works on your route.
You can now choose a safe way to get paid by a buyer in another country and spot the signs of a payment scam.

check.q: A new buyer in Abidjan sends a screenshot saying he paid. What do you do before sending goods?
options: Check your own balance to confirm the money arrived
Send him your PIN so he can check
check.why: Screenshots can be fake; only your own balance proves the money arrived.

check.q: A buyer says he sent too much and asks you to send back the difference. What is this most likely?
options: A bank error you must fix fast
A common scam: check your balance and talk to your provider
check.why: "I sent too much, send it back" is a well-known scam; check your balance and call your provider's official number.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Unofficial charges, delays and your trade plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Describe the safe steps to take when asked for an unofficial payment, and report it as a non-tariff barrier.
This lesson builds toward: When someone at or near the border asks for an unofficial payment or holds your goods, you will describe the safe steps to take and report the problem as a non-tariff barrier, naming the official reporting channel and the facts to write down.
A non-tariff barrier (NTB) is anything other than a duty that makes trade harder: unofficial charges at roadblocks, long delays, papers that are not in the rules, or goods held without a reason. The AfCFTA has an online system, tradebarriers.africa, where any trader, including informal traders, women and young people, can report an NTB. Reports go to national focal points and the AfCFTA Secretariat to be followed up.
If someone asks for money without a receipt: stay calm and polite, and put your safety first. Ask for the official fee and a receipt. Ask to speak to the officer in charge, or to the trade information desk. Do not argue in a way that puts you in danger.
Afterwards, write the facts: date, time, place, what was asked, the amount, and any name or badge number you saw. Report it on tradebarriers.africa (online or through its mobile phone option), to your customs authority's complaints line, or through your traders' association. Women traders who face harassment can also ask their association or a women traders' group for support.
Now put it all together. Your cross-border trade plan has: the product and crossing, the rules you checked, your papers, your cost and price in two currencies, how you get paid, and what you will do about unofficial charges.
Step by step:
- Stay calm and polite; your safety comes first.
- Ask for the official fee and a receipt, or for the officer in charge or the trade desk.
- Write the facts: date, time, place, amount, name or badge number.
- Report it on tradebarriers.africa, to customs, or through your traders' association.
- Add these steps to your cross-border trade plan.
Words to know:
- Non-tariff barrier (NTB): anything other than a duty that makes trade harder, like unofficial charges, long delays or extra papers.
- Focal point: the person or office in each country that follows up NTB reports.
Official sources:
- AfCFTA Non-Tariff Barriers reporting, monitoring and elimination mechanism
- AfCFTA Secretariat: About the AfCFTA (55 AU countries, trading from 1 January 2021, Secretariat in Accra)
Try it now: Write your one-page cross-border trade plan, as described in the final task. Add the facts you would write down and where you would report an unofficial charge.
You can now deal safely with an unofficial charge, report it as a non-tariff barrier, and write a full cross-border trade plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Rules checked The plan says nothing about which rules apply, or relies on a rumour. The plan names the regional scheme or AfCFTA rule for the route and at least two offices or websites to check with. It also records what an office said, with the date and the officer's name. Papers listed No list of papers, or only an ID. A list of the papers for this product and route, including an invoice and a customs declaration, and a certificate of origin where a lower duty is wanted. It also notes any health, plant or product certificate and how copies are kept. Full cost and price Only the cost of the goods is counted, or the arithmetic is wrong. Every cost is listed, the cost per item and selling price are correct, and the price is shown in both currencies. It also compares the price with the buyer's market and allows for a change in the exchange rate. Safe payment Goods are released before payment is checked, or the plan shares a PIN. A safe method is named, goods are released only after the balance is checked, and no PIN is ever shared. It also lists the scam warning signs the trader will watch for. Unofficial charges No plan, or the plan is to pay and say nothing. Safe steps, the facts to write down and an official reporting channel are named. It names two reporting channels and a traders' association for support. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of your plan and try again.

check.q: Where can a small trader report an unofficial charge at an African border?
options: tradebarriers.africa, customs or a traders' association
To the person who asked for the money
check.why: The AfCFTA NTB system, customs complaints lines and traders' associations are the official routes.

check.q: What should you write down after an unofficial charge?
options: The date, time, place, amount and any name or badge number
The price of your goods only
check.why: Clear facts make a report that can be followed up.
